vignette:
Amina is an 80-year-old widow who has spent much of her later life working as a policy analyst, known by colleagues for her precision, composure, and ability to sit through long meetings without losing the thread. She came to treatment after a life-threatening motor vehicle collision that occurred several months ago and has remained sharply present in her daily life in ways that feel to her both unpredictable and overpowering. Before the crash, she described herself as self-contained and disciplined. Since it, she has felt as though ordinary sensations in the world can seize hold of her without warning.

The collision happened while she was riding in a car on a cold day, the kind of day when the air through a cracked window leaves a distinct chill across the skin. She remembers certain fragments with painful sharpness: the sudden recognition that something was wrong, the violent movement of vehicles around her, the smell that followed in the aftermath, and the sense that her body was no longer under her control. Other parts are absent. She can describe one instant in exact detail and then comes to a blank stretch she cannot fill in, as if the sequence has been torn. What is especially distressing to her is that the memory does not return gradually. A sensation or smell in the present can bring it back all at once, complete and immediate, before she has any chance to prepare herself. At other times, she feels herself force the memory away midstream, stopping it before it fully forms because she cannot bear where it is going.

The sensory reminders have become central features of her days. A brief change in temperature against her skin can transport her. If a draft hits her forearm in an over-air-conditioned conference room, or if she steps from a warm hallway into winter air outside the office, she can suddenly feel as if she is back at the scene rather than in the present. The smell of alcohol is especially potent. Passing a colleague with hand sanitizer still wet on their palms, or catching the sharp scent of disinfectant in an elevator, can make her body react before she has put words to what is happening. Burnt smells are similarly alarming; once, when something scorched in the office kitchenette, she froze in the corridor, heart racing, overwhelmed by the conviction that she was again in immediate danger. In those moments she does not simply remember the crash. She can feel as if it is happening again, reacting to the present as though it were the collision itself.

Since the accident, she has also become intensely watchful of movement around her. In the office, if someone rises abruptly from a chair or gestures suddenly across the table, she goes instantly on guard. She finds herself tracking people’s motions with a vigilance that is exhausting and difficult to conceal. During a recent policy meeting, a coworker reached quickly across her line of sight to hand over a folder, and Amina jerked back so sharply that the room went quiet. She later felt ashamed of how visible her fear had become, but in the moment she was certain she needed to protect herself. Strong emotions come on with very little notice: fear most often, but also horror, anger, guilt, and shame, sometimes all tangled together. She has struggled to explain these reactions to others because from the outside the triggers seem so minor, while to her they carry the full force of the crash.

Over the following weeks and months, she began arranging her life to limit these encounters. She avoids rooms that are kept too cold and hesitates near communal spaces where she might smell hand sanitizer, cleaning products, or burnt food. She has become careful about where she sits in meetings, preferring places where other people’s movements are easier to monitor. Even with these precautions, reminders still break through. When they do, she may lose her sense of the room for a moment and then work hard to compose herself, pressing the memory down before it can fully unfold. The effort of doing this repeatedly has narrowed her world. She remains employed, but work has become more effortful and socially fraught, and she has begun turning down collaborative tasks that would once have suited her well.

What finally brought her to seek help was not a single episode but the cumulative realization that she was organizing more and more of her life around avoiding the next abrupt sensory jolt. She was troubled by how quickly she could be pulled out of the present and by how little command she had over when the memory arrived. At 80, she said, she had expected to be using her remaining years with deliberateness, not bracing herself against cold air, sharp smells, and sudden gestures. What frightens her most is the feeling that the world can change in an instant and that her body will know it before her mind does. What she hopes for, cautiously, is not to erase what happened but to be able to sit in a meeting, walk through her office, or feel winter air on her skin without being thrown back into the collision.
